Question: Let \(L_n\) denote the least common multiple of the numbers \(1,\) \(2,\) \(3,\) \(\ldots,\) \(n,\) and let \(h\) be the unique positive integer such that \[\dfrac{1}{1} + \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{17} = \dfrac{h}{L_{17}}\] What is the remainder when \(h\) is divided by \(17?\)
Solution:
Write all terms over the common denominator \(L_{17}\). For every denominator \(j\le16\), the integer \(L_{17}/j\) still contains a factor of \(17\). Only the numerator contributed by \(1/17\) can affect the remainder modulo \(17\).

We write \(u\equiv v\pmod{17}\) when \(u-v\) is a multiple of \(17\); the two integers then have the same remainder on division by \(17\).

Because \(17\) is prime and is absent from \(L_{16}\), we have \(L_{17}=17L_{16}\). Thus
\[
h\equiv L_{17}/17=L_{16}\pmod{17}.
\]
To be divisible by every integer from \(1\) through \(16\), the least common multiple needs the largest available power of each prime:
\[
L_{16}=2^4\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13.
\]
Reduce in small groups. Modulo \(17\), \(2^4\equiv-1\), \(5\cdot7\equiv1\), \(9\cdot11\equiv-3\), and \(13\equiv-4\). Their product is congruent to \((-1)(1)(-3)(-4)=-12\equiv5\).

Adding \(17\) to \(-12\) gives the usual nonnegative remainder \(5\), without changing its remainder class. The remainder is \(\boxed{5}\), choice C. A remainder question can let most terms disappear before any large common denominator is calculated.
